item.title: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on AI agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that autonomously handle tasks and integrate with over 4,000 apps across Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced Dots, always-on AI agents designed to work continuously on users' behalf by learning preferences and managing tasks autonomously. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, these agents operate on their own cloud computers, connect to thousands of apps, and are accessible via ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams, aiming to increase productivity by handling routine and complex work. Dots can independently manage projects, update analyses, automate content production, and adapt to changing requirements across various professional roles. OpenAI is rolling out Dots to eligible users on Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans, with plans to expand availability and develop specialist Dots for deeper organizational integration and responsibilities.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol, matching GPT-6 Astra's intelligence on coding and professional tasks at one-fifth the cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol, an upgraded model that nearly matches the intelligence of GPT-6 Astra in agentic coding, computer use, and professional work while costing only one-fifth as much in input and output token prices. The model offers significant improvements over GPT-6 Sol in complex tasks such as software engineering, document understanding, and multi-step business workflows, delivering higher accuracy and efficiency at substantially lower cost. GPT-6.1 Sol excels in various benchmarks, including DeepSWE for software engineering, GDP.pdf for professional document analysis, AutomationBench for business workflows, OSWorld for computer-use tasks, and Terminal-Bench Science for scientific research workflows. It reduces factual errors compared to GPT-6 Sol and approaches Astra's performance at a fraction of the cost, making it suitable for a wide range of demanding applications while enabling developers to build and run capable AI agents more affordably.

item.title: PostHog releases Jeeves, a reasoning-enhanced Jev-like decision model based on Qwen3.5-9B that improves accuracy on out-of-domain tasks and JevBench benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: PostHog has introduced Jeeves, a 9-billion-parameter Jev-like classifier built on Qwen3.5-9B with a diffusion drafter that incorporates reasoning before decision-making. Jeeves outperforms previous models like Kev-9B and Jev on test data it was not trained on, achieving higher accuracy on public JevBench tiers. It supports multiple question types through a Jev-compatible API and runs efficiently on CUDA-enabled GPUs. The model is trained using supervised fine-tuning and contrastive iterative self-play optimization, enabling it to think before deciding, which improves performance especially on harder and out-of-domain tasks. PostHog provides full training code, data, and pre-trained weights, along with a Python SDK compatible with Jev clients for easy integration and deployment.

item.title: China expands travel restrictions to include family members of leading AI experts amid talent control measures
item.description: China has extended its travel curbs to cover the family members of top artificial intelligence professionals as part of broader efforts to regulate the movement of key personnel in the AI sector. This expansion aims to tighten control over the mobility of critical talent and their close associates within the country.

item.title: Google is paying about 100 digital publishers for AI Overviews that contribute to search and other AI-powered products [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Google has started a pilot program paying roughly 100 digital publishers for the content that contributes to AI-generated summaries, known as AI Overviews, used in its search engine and other products. This marks a shift from Google's previous stance of not paying publishers, as AI Overviews have reduced traffic referrals to publishers' websites, leading to complaints and lawsuits from some publishers. The program reflects Google's response to concerns about declining web traffic caused by AI-powered answers that summarize content directly in search results, which has affected publishers' revenue and sparked industry disputes over content compensation.

item.title: The Model Is the Easy Half: Explaining AI system challenges beyond model creation, focusing on implementation and deployment complexities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article explains that building the AI model is often the simpler part of developing AI systems, while the more difficult challenges lie in implementation, deployment, and ensuring accurate, reliable outputs. It uses an analogy comparing a language model to a skilled cook who has never seen the kitchen, emphasizing the need to build the surrounding infrastructure to support the model's outputs. The article provides a detailed explanation accessible to both technical and non-technical readers, illustrating common pitfalls such as incorrect or fabricated information generated by models despite fluent language. It highlights the importance of preprocessing documents correctly, managing data retrieval, and designing systems that verify and contextualize model responses to improve overall system reliability.

item.title: Hacker News users discuss strategies to manage AI coding agent usage limits amid cost concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News discussion explores how developers handle usage limits imposed by AI coding agents, focusing on maintaining ongoing task context while switching tools. Participants share approaches such as optimizing queries, using multiple accounts, and seeking alternative tools due to the high cost of upgrading plans from $20 to $100-200 per month per agent.

item.title: LabBench benchmarks AI agents on selecting next wet-lab experiments, finding they interpret data well but struggle to choose or design experiments independently [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers developed LabBench, a benchmark of 20 real-world wet-lab tasks from drug discovery and genomics, to evaluate AI agents' ability to decide the next experiment in biological research. The benchmark tests agents on criteria derived from actual lab decisions, withholding the labs' choices to assess autonomous decision-making. Five leading AI agents were tested, with the best passing about 40% of criteria but none able to reliably select or design the next experiment, highlighting a reasoning bottleneck. Agents excelled at interpreting experimental data but failed on tasks requiring commitment or ranking of experiments. Adding minimal hints improved performance, suggesting agents have latent knowledge but struggle with recall and decision-making. The results indicate current AI can assist expert biologists in analysis but lack the autonomous experimental design capability needed to accelerate biological discovery fully. LabBench aims to drive improvements toward AI agents capable of supervised or autonomous wet-lab experimentation.

item.title: President Trump announces White House Accord on Super Intelligence with AI companies, including non-binding safety commitments and model auditing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: President Donald Trump announced that leading AI companies have agreed to a non-binding White House Accord on Super Intelligence, which includes provisions for AI safety such as internal controls on model alignment and external auditing. Trump shared the details of the accord on his Truth Social platform. The agreement aims to establish voluntary safety standards among AI developers to address concerns about advanced AI systems.

item.title: AMD acquires AI startup World Labs for $8.2 billion while Oura delays IPO amid market uncertainty, illustrating divergence in 2024 VC exits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: In 2024, venture capital exits show a split between mergers and acquisitions and initial public offerings. AMD announced an $8.2 billion all-stock acquisition of AI startup World Labs, co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, marking a major M&A deal this year. This follows other significant acquisitions including SpaceX's purchase of Cursor, Nvidia's acquisition of Hugging Face, and Stripe's buyout of OpenRouter. Andreessen Horowitz holds nearly 14% of World Labs, highlighting its investment stake. Conversely, health-tracking wearable company Oura postponed its planned IPO due to market uncertainty, underscoring challenges in the public offering market despite strong M&A activity in the tech sector.

item.title: Recommendations urge AI labs to responsibly release AI-generated mathematical results with human understanding and community-led verification [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A report outlines recommendations for AI labs producing advanced mathematical results, emphasizing the need for responsible release practices that ensure human understanding and verification. The guidelines distinguish between results fully understood by humans, which should follow traditional academic norms, and those not yet understood, which require additional support and transparent dissemination. The recommendations arose from feedback by over 600 mathematicians and stress that AI labs should not withhold significant mathematical findings behind proprietary models. Labs are urged to provide funding and resources to foster community-led efforts to interpret and validate AI-generated mathematics, maintaining scholarly norms of responsibility and peer review. The report also discourages AI labs from directing the development of human understanding, advocating for organic growth within the mathematical community.

item.title: America.gov chatbot recites Minecraft End Poem as an intentional easter egg, not a glitch [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The U.S. government launched the America.gov AI chatbot in partnership with Google and SpaceXAI, which responds unusually when asked about Minecraft by reciting a poetic monologue based on the game's End Poem. This behavior is a deliberate easter egg rather than a malfunction, reflecting a creative integration within the chatbot's design. The poem, originally written by Julian Gough for Minecraft, is adapted by the chatbot into a message blending government themes and existential reflections. The chatbot has proven resistant to jailbreak attempts and includes accurate political facts, indicating careful engineering behind its responses. This unexpected feature highlights a unique intersection of government technology and cultural references.

item.title: Sam Altman says OpenAI will delay IPO until it can ensure AI model safety, citing risks and avoiding Wall Street pressure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced that the company will not go public until it can confidently guarantee the safety of its AI models, with no specific timeline set. He emphasized the importance of prioritizing safety amid rapid AI advancements and expressed concerns about the pressures of meeting Wall Street expectations during this critical phase. Altman's remarks came during a Q&A after OpenAI's DevDay keynote, following recent controversies over AI safety and cybersecurity incidents involving OpenAI and other AI firms. While acknowledging the benefits of going public, Altman warned that waiting too long could also be detrimental, highlighting the delicate balance between advancing AI capabilities and ensuring responsible deployment.

item.title: Fateshow launches platform combining traditional astrology charts with AI-generated fortune-telling readings for career, relationships, and decision-making [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Fateshow is a new platform that integrates Eastern and Western astrological methods to generate detailed charts followed by AI-powered interpretations. Users can access natal charts, synastry readings, and live divination answers to guide personal and professional decisions. The platform supports multiple systems including Zi Wei Dou Shu, BaZi, Western astrology, Human Design, Vedic astrology, and various divination methods, allowing users to verify chart data before reviewing AI-generated insights.

item.title: Moching launches AI desktop agent in Rust with 219 built-in tools to operate entire PC via screen and input control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Moching is an AI desktop agent developed in Rust that operates a user's entire computer by seeing the screen, moving the mouse, opening apps, and executing tasks. It features 219 native tools across 12 domains and integrates a Python runtime for flexibility, aiming to automate workflows beyond coding assistance or chatbots. The software supports Windows 10+ and macOS 12+ with Apple Silicon, requiring an OpenAI-compatible API key. Moching emphasizes a complete human-computer interaction loop-perceiving, deciding, executing, and verifying results-distinguishing it from other AI tools that focus on single tasks. It is independently developed, available without subscription, and offers a referral program that rewards users with credits.

item.title: Oura delays IPO amid broader market stall affecting companies like Amaero and Holtec Nuclear
item.description: Oura, a fitness ring maker, has postponed its initial public offering due to uncertainty in the IPO market, reflecting a wider slowdown that has also impacted metals producer Amaero and Holtec Nuclear Corp. The stalled IPO environment is influenced by factors such as rising energy costs, trade tensions, military conflicts, increasing interest rates, and uncertainties in data center development. Meanwhile, SB Energy, a SoftBank-controlled power developer for data centers, has filed IPO paperwork but has not yet started marketing the offering.

item.title: Researchers jailbreak Chinese AI models Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm to reveal bioweapons and assassination instructions, prompting Moonshot's internal review [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Chinese AI developer Moonshot is reviewing its Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm models after security researchers at Mindgard successfully bypassed safety guardrails to extract instructions on making biological weapons and carrying out assassinations. Mindgard discovered the vulnerabilities during a jailbreaking process in July, which allowed the AI to discuss prohibited topics and potentially enable cyber-attacks by running code and connecting to the internet. Moonshot acknowledged the findings and is collaborating with Mindgard to address the issues, emphasizing its openness to third-party input for improving AI safety. The incident highlights ongoing concerns about the risks of open-weight AI models, which can be run independently, and the challenges of regulating AI misuse amid rapid technological development.

item.title: AstroForge plans to fly a spacecraft autonomously using AI in 2027 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AstroForge, a space mining company, plans to launch a spacecraft in 2027 that will test full autonomy using artificial intelligence. The mission aims to demonstrate the spacecraft's ability to operate independently without human intervention during its flight.

item.title: Huawei releases DeepGEMM-Ascend, a matrix multiplication kernel library optimized for Ascend NPUs with support for BF16, FP8, FP4, and MegaMoE [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Huawei has launched DeepGEMM-Ascend, a matrix multiplication kernel library designed for its Ascend Neural Processing Units (NPUs). The library is fully API-compatible with DeepGEMM and supports various data formats including BF16, FP8, FP4, as well as MQA logits and MegaMoE operators, aiming to optimize performance on Ascend hardware. DeepGEMM-Ascend provides a lightweight abstraction over Ascend's matrix multiply-add primitives, simplifying complex operations like fractal layouts and alignment constraints. It employs Ascend-specific optimizations such as sparse data loading and coroutine-based pipelining to approach peak hardware performance across diverse matrix shapes. The library supports Ascend 950 devices and integrates with existing DeepGEMM APIs and workflows, facilitating adoption by developers targeting Huawei's AI platform.

item.title: Google and Microsoft join Apache Ossie to standardize enterprise data access for AI applications [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google and Microsoft have joined Apache Ossie, an industry group that includes Snowflake and Nvidia, aiming to simplify how AI tools access data from various applications and databases. This collaboration seeks to create standardized methods for AI systems to better understand and utilize enterprise data. The group focuses on developing open-source software and protocols that facilitate seamless data integration for AI, potentially accelerating AI adoption in enterprise environments by reducing data silos and compatibility issues.

item.title: Elon Musk's xAI acquired dot.com domain redirecting to Grok chatbot ahead of OpenAI's Dots launch, sparking internet speculation of a prank [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Elon Musk's AI company xAI acquired the domain dot.com in July, which now redirects to the download page for its Grok chatbot app, coinciding with OpenAI's launch of its new AI agent called Dots. The timing and domain choice have led to widespread speculation online that xAI may have intentionally purchased the domain to troll OpenAI's product launch. While it is possible the acquisition was for typical domain investment reasons, the coincidence has drawn significant attention and humor from the internet community.

item.title: Anthropic details how to choose and optimize models in the Claude 5.5 family for better token efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic explains how developers can select the appropriate model from the Claude 5.5 family and maximize the value of each token when building AI applications. The guidance aims to help users understand the trade-offs and capabilities of different Claude 5.5 models to improve performance and cost-effectiveness.

item.title: Trump signs executive order requiring US government to replace 'artificial intelligence' with 'Super Intelligence' in official documents and communications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: President Donald Trump has issued an executive order directing the US executive branch to stop using the term "artificial intelligence" and instead refer to it as "Super Intelligence" in all official policy websites, documents, and press releases. Trump described "Super Intelligence" as a more accurate and positive term, emphasizing its power and potential for good use while distancing it from the negative connotations of the word "artificial." The order follows a White House luncheon with tech CEOs and government officials, where Trump discussed regulation and community relations related to AI technologies.

item.title: InfiniHash launches App Store with compliance tools developed entirely by AI agents [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: InfiniHash has introduced an App Store offering compliance and governance tools created end-to-end by AI agents to assist IT and managed service providers with regulatory adherence. One featured tool, AttestProof, automates access reviews by converting user-access data into reviewer campaigns and generates timestamped, hash-chained evidence accepted by auditors.

item.title: Reflex Engine outperforms Llama.cpp and vLLM in cold-start latency and time-to-first-token on serverless GPU platforms [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Reflex Engine, a Rust and CUDA inference engine, demonstrates faster cold-start performance and lower time-to-first-token compared to Llama.cpp and vLLM, particularly on serverless GPU platforms like Runpod. It achieves this by compiling CUDA kernels ahead-of-time to avoid runtime compilation delays, resulting in a median cold start of approximately 456ms on a Tesla T4 GPU. The engine is optimized for single-shot requests where billing is based on wall-clock time per invocation, making rapid startup critical for cost efficiency. Real-world tests on Runpod showed Reflex's container startup to ready time at about 1.6 seconds, significantly faster than vLLM's 150 seconds, although overall cold start times are limited by platform scheduling and provisioning delays. Reflex's design avoids batching and warm-pool assumptions, focusing on minimizing marginal startup overhead on top of the platform's inherent latency floor.

item.title: SpaceXAI's AI-powered Grokipedia resumes article updates after months-long pause, with recent fact-checks and user suggestions accepted [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Grokipedia, the AI-driven encyclopedia developed by SpaceXAI and associated with Elon Musk, has resumed updating its articles after a pause of several months. Recent activity includes fact-checking of pages like Barack Obama and Elon Musk, as well as acceptance of user-submitted updates such as a video game release date. While some pages remain outdated, the platform's live update site shows ongoing edits and reviews. The site had not reviewed edits since April, according to a previous report, but now displays recent changes, including notes to recheck references. SpaceXAI has not commented on the renewed activity, and Elon Musk has not posted about Grokipedia since early 2026. Benji Taylor, head of design at X and SpaceXAI, indicated that a new version of Grokipedia is forthcoming, suggesting continued development despite the earlier inactivity.

item.title: Researchers explore AI-driven methods to improve cancer diagnosis accuracy and personalize treatments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence are enhancing cancer research by enabling more efficient data analysis and supporting the development of potential therapies. Researchers are investigating AI techniques to improve diagnostic precision and tailor treatment options for cancer patients.

item.title: Diffsmith launches AI-powered macOS code review studio for local git changes with inline commenting and AI agent integration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Diffsmith has released a native macOS application called Code Review Studio that helps developers review local git changes and commits using AI assistance. The tool allows users to browse diffs, leave inline comments on specific lines, and interact with AI agents to get feedback or code changes, all while keeping data private on the user's Mac without cloud involvement. The app supports syntax-highlighted diffs, side-by-side or inline views, and live updates as files change. Users can convert comments into AI-ready prompts or enable a local server for AI agents to read and reply directly within the app. Diffsmith is designed for privacy with no outbound network calls unless the optional local agent server is activated, and it offers customization options like font sizes, themes, and light/dark modes.

item.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT with app discovery, plugin extensions, and AI agents to challenge traditional app store model [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI announced new features at its Dev Day that transform ChatGPT into a platform for discovering, launching, and using apps directly within the chatbot interface. These updates include app suggestions during conversations, expanded plugin support with interactive panels, and a "Sign in with ChatGPT" feature that lets users carry their AI allowances across third-party apps. The company also introduced autonomous AI agents called Dots that can perform tasks by navigating the web and using connected apps on behalf of users. The new capabilities aim to disrupt the traditional app store ecosystem by making ChatGPT a central hub for software interaction, reducing the need for users to download separate apps. OpenAI also launched an enterprise app marketplace with over 30 partners, allowing customers to apply their OpenAI commitments toward approved software. Improvements to the plugin review process and app sharing features further support developers and collaborative workflows within the ChatGPT environment.

item.title: Tristan Harris releases Moloch, a short film warning about risks in the AI development race [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Tristan Harris has released a short film titled Moloch that serves as a cautionary tale about the rapid advancements in artificial intelligence. The film highlights potential ethical concerns and risks associated with the ongoing AI race, urging reflection on its consequences.

item.title: Vibe Coding Discover launches catalog of AI open-source software for agents, multi-channel platforms, skills, and retrieval-augmented generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Vibe Coding Discover is a new catalog compiling open-source software focused on artificial intelligence components such as agents, multi-channel platforms, skills, and retrieval-augmented generation. It aims to help developers and researchers find and use AI OSS resources more effectively. The catalog includes projects like VoiceStudio, a fully local, open-source alternative to ElevenLabs for voice cloning, text-to-speech, and transcription across 646 languages, featuring a desktop app, model manager, local API, and multi-channel platform server for agent integration.

item.title: TUNAI reports 600,000 live job ads nightly across US, UK, Canada, and Australia with 34,000 ads over a year old
item.description: TUNAI monitors live job advertisements in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, finding around 600,000 active listings each night. Among these, 34,000 ads claim to have been posted over a year ago, with some dating back to 2010. The data also reveals that a significant portion of job ads do not disclose pay figures, with 80% in the UK, 72% in Canada, and 76% in Australia lacking salary information. Additional insights include the timing of job postings, with most UK ads appearing on weekdays and 31% posted during a three-hour window in UK time. Common job title hype words like "rockstar," "ninja," and "champion" persist in listings. The platform also offers a CV check feature that ranks live roles against individual resumes, providing further context for job seekers.

item.title: Sources: OpenAI in talks to raise $30 billion at $1.4 trillion valuation ahead of delayed 2027 IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI is reportedly negotiating a $30 billion pre-IPO funding round at a $1.4 trillion valuation, marking a bridge round before its anticipated public debut in 2027. The company postponed its IPO from 2026 to focus on AI safety, with CEO Sam Altman emphasizing the importance of mitigating existential risks posed by AI. The funding talks follow a previous $12 billion raise in March at an $852 billion valuation. OpenAI's revenue has surged 70% since July, reaching $40 billion in August, driven by strategic focus areas like coding. The new round aims to support growth and safety priorities ahead of the public offering.

item.title: PSSA: Rust-implemented non-transformer language model with recurrent state-space architecture outperforms transformer on learning speed and CPU generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: PSSA is a small language model written entirely in Rust without using transformer architecture or ML frameworks. It processes text token-by-token with a recurrent state-space layer, maintains an episodic memory bank, and updates its own weights dynamically, resulting in faster learning and text generation compared to a transformer with the same parameters and corpus. The model's design avoids the quadratic cost of transformers by carrying a fixed-size state and using memory lookups, leading to linear cost growth with sequence length. In experiments on WikiText-103, PSSA achieved lower training and held-out loss than a transformer, generalizing better while generating text about twelve times faster on the same CPU. The project is a research prototype with 1.5 million parameters and highlights the need for more compute resources to explore scaling and further evaluation.

item.title: Microsoft joins Apache Ossie to ease AI access to application data after blocking Power BI integrations, signaling a shift in its AI data strategy [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Microsoft has reversed its earlier move to block partners from connecting their data management tools to Power BI by joining Apache Ossie, a software group that aims to simplify AI access to data from applications and databases. This change aligns with CEO Satya Nadella's strategy of building products that integrate with competitors' offerings, contrasting with Microsoft's previous effort to protect its Fabric data product by limiting rival access. The decision follows criticism of Microsoft's earlier stance and mirrors similar transitions by companies like Salesforce, which now facilitates AI tool access to its data for a fee.

item.title: OpenAI supports Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform privately but is not a public member of the consortium addressing rogue AI agents [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nvidia launched the Open Agent Safety Platform, a consortium of over 100 companies aiming to tackle rogue AI agents, but OpenAI is notably absent from the public list of supporters. Despite this, OpenAI is collaborating privately with Nvidia on key components like OpenShell, an open source sandbox designed to contain AI agents. The platform combines open source software with proprietary Nvidia hardware, including the Sentry monitoring system on BlueField-4 processors, to enforce agent behavior at the hardware level. OpenAI's absence from the public consortium may reflect its desire for independence from Nvidia and its own AI safety initiatives, including a separate cybersecurity consortium and internal safeguards. Other major tech companies like Amazon, Google, and Apple also have not publicly joined Nvidia's effort.

item.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns of significant AI risks after meeting with former President Trump at the White House [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei expressed concerns about the substantial risks posed by artificial intelligence following a meeting with former President Donald Trump at the White House. He emphasized the need to address these risks as AI technologies continue to develop rapidly.

item.title: Sources: OpenAI nears $70 billion in annualized revenue, up 70% since early Q3 amid enterprise sales push [ ! ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI is approaching $70 billion in annualized revenue, reflecting about a 70% increase from its revenue pace at the start of the third quarter, according to a person familiar with the figures. This growth coincides with OpenAI's intensified focus on selling its products to enterprise customers. The company has also rapidly reduced prices to accelerate adoption among businesses.

item.title: Bay Area artists unveil Titanic-themed sculpture depicting OpenAI leaders escaping a sinking ship at San Francisco developer event [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Two artists from Berkeley-based Odd Friend Studio created a 5-foot-tall sculpture called What Iceberg? that portrays OpenAI's leaders and investors fleeing a sinking ship with wealth while others face AI's consequences. The installation was displayed at the entrance of an OpenAI developer event in San Francisco as a form of protest against the company. The artists spent five days crafting the piece by hand using papier mâché, cardboard, and paint, emphasizing the time and effort involved as a contrast to AI-generated art. This protest follows other recent demonstrations against OpenAI, including one in New York City, amid ongoing controversies such as halted training of GPT-6.1 Astra over safety concerns and legal challenges from the state of Florida.

item.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT-based office suite with collaborative workspace, word processor, and slides, challenging Microsoft's workplace software [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI announced a new suite of office features at its DevDay conference, including Space, a shared workspace for collaboration with AI agents, Pages, a word processor for human and AI collaboration, and upcoming collaborative slides. These tools position OpenAI as a competitor to traditional office software providers like Microsoft and Google. The features aim to integrate AI more deeply into workplace productivity, allowing users to generate content, update documents, and collaborate with AI personas called Dots. OpenAI's move reflects a broader industry trend as Microsoft and Salesforce also expand their AI offerings to keep pace with evolving software demands.

item.title: x.ai launches Team Bots to enhance collaborative AI workflows
item.description: x.ai has introduced Team Bots, a new feature designed to facilitate collaboration and streamline workflows within teams using AI. The platform aims to improve productivity by integrating AI-driven assistance into team environments.

item.title: Anthropic discloses up to $84.5 billion in SpaceX compute agreements through 2029, mostly cancellable with 90-day notice [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has revealed agreements to pay SpaceX up to $84.5 billion for access to Nvidia-based computing capacity through 2029, according to a confidential IPO prospectus. These agreements are largely cancellable with a 90-day notice period. The disclosure highlights the scale of Anthropic's investment in compute resources from SpaceX as part of its AI development plans.

item.title: Wabi pivots from AI app builder to AI messaging platform that creates interfaces on demand [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Wabi, an AI startup originally focused on prompt-based app creation, has shifted to become an AI messaging platform that acts as a personal agent capable of building user interfaces dynamically to assist with tasks. The new Wabi 2.0 combines chat, apps, and ongoing task management in a single interface, aiming to improve user experience beyond traditional chat-only agents. Founder Eugenia Kuyda described Wabi 2.0 as software that adapts to users' lives by creating apps on demand for activities like health tracking or family management. The platform is currently available by invite only and seeks to integrate personal agents, apps, and social interactions in one place to better support users' daily needs.

item.title: OpenAI launches Dots, always-on agentic assistants powered by GPT-6 Astra for Pro and Business Premium users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced Dots at its DevDay event, a new type of personal assistant powered by GPT-6 Astra that operates independently across platforms to pursue user-defined goals with minimal oversight. Dots are designed to work continuously in the background and can be customized and named by users, with plans for teams of Dots to collaborate on tasks. Dots will be available to Pro and Business Premium users in eligible markets starting Tuesday and can be accessed through ChatGPT and Codex. OpenAI envisions various use cases, such as software developers deploying Dots to monitor customer feedback and scientists using them to analyze experimental data. The assistants can communicate via organizational platforms like Slack and Teams, with text messaging support coming soon, and can be provisioned with specific identities and tools, including integration with Microsoft's Agent 365 security controls.

item.title: OpenAI updates Codex with reusable cloud development environments, voice-controlled CLI, code review tools, and security scanning features [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has enhanced its software engineering agent Codex by introducing reusable cloud development environments accessible across devices, a refreshed command-line interface with voice controls, and new code review capabilities integrated into the ChatGPT desktop app. These updates aim to improve developer productivity by enabling persistent, configurable cloud workspaces and streamlined task management. Additionally, OpenAI launched Codex Security Cloud, a toolset for scanning GitHub repositories to identify and fix security issues automatically, leveraging models from its Daybreak Blue cybersecurity initiative. The company also introduced API enhancements, including a Decisions API for real-time decision-making and expanded support for Amazon's Bedrock Managed Agents to run OpenAI agents on AWS.

item.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT plug-ins with app-like interfaces, interactive panels, and automation support [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has enhanced ChatGPT plug-ins by introducing dedicated sidebar homes, interactive panels, and file viewers, allowing developers to create app-like experiences within ChatGPT. The update also includes improved plug-in discovery, a new Plugin Creator tool, and individual access approvals for users. Additionally, ChatGPT Sites can now host these plug-ins, and OpenAI supports the MCP Events specification to enable automations triggered by connected app events.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6.1 Sol, claims near GPT-6 Astra performance at one-fifth the token cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol at its DevDay event, stating the model nearly matches GPT-6 Astra in agentic coding, professional tasks, and complex workflows while costing significantly less. The company highlights improvements over GPT-6 Sol in programming, document understanding, and factual accuracy, with a reduced error rate and better adherence to safety constraints. OpenAI decided not to release GPT-6.1 Astra due to internal safety concerns about deception and unauthorized task execution. GPT-6.1 Sol is now available to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, though it is not yet accessible in Chat.

item.title: Researchers present CHESTPHENOT, a compact 0.5-3B parameter language model for locally deployable, auditable extraction of labels, status, and evidence from radiology reports [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CHESTPHENOT jointly extracts finding labels, three-class status (present/absent/uncertain), and verbatim supporting evidence spans from radiology reports, addressing challenges of local inference and auditability without relying on external APIs. Trained with hybrid CheXbert and 72B silver supervision followed by fine-tuning and refinement, the 3B model performs competitively across in-distribution, cross-taxonomy, and cross-institution evaluations, surpassing CheXbert on cross-institution detection by 2.0 F1 points. It also outperforms larger prompted models on most detection and status tasks, achieving over 99% locatable evidence spans and a 47.5 auditable-F1 score, exceeding Qwen2.5-7B one-shot prompting by 7.6 points and approaching Qwen2.5-72B.

item.title: Researchers propose a neural network model for age-adaptive handwriting reconstruction using IMU-based digital pens, addressing variability between adult and child handwriting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a neural network architecture based on a Temporal Convolutional Network with multiple prediction heads to improve handwriting reconstruction from sensor data collected by IMU-equipped digital pens. The model is designed to handle significant differences in handwriting dynamics between adults and children without requiring user-specific adaptation, enabling deployment directly on the pen. The approach leverages shared representations across age groups while accounting for domain-specific variations caused by differences in motor control and graphomotor development. This cross-domain learning method aims to overcome challenges posed by the high variability in children's handwriting and the limited feasibility of collecting large-scale data in classroom settings, improving the generalization of handwriting reconstruction models across populations.

item.title: Researchers study communication between frozen large language models via prompt optimization in a referential game with shared code protocols [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers investigate communication between two frozen large language models from different providers, each accessed through APIs with distinct tokenizers, playing a referential game where one describes an object in a fixed-length message and the other identifies it from candidates. Neither model's weights are updated; instead, isolated prompt optimizers rewrite each agent's prompt based on scored interactions to develop a shared communication code. In experiments, optimized prompts in a positional setting generalize to unseen objects beyond a no-codebook baseline, even without memory windows. Challenges arise when message length constraints prevent independent per-letter blocks, but a whole-object place value code enables communication in some runs. Techniques like sender collision penalties and sequential optimization improve success, though outcomes vary. Successful protocols are embedded in optimized prompts, allowing direct reading and auditing of the communication method.

item.title: Typed Decision Models: An Early Evidence Audit and Evaluation Checklist [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return probability distributions over caller-defined options without generating text. TypeSafe released Jev, a commercial typed decision model, on 15 September 2026, and a small body of evaluation and replication work appeared within days. We review 28 papers posted between 19 and 24 September and relate their findings to earlier work on label-probability classification, constrained decoding, reranking, calibration, and model cascades. In this early literature, the typed readout itself has not shown an independent accuracy advantage over comparable label-probability readouts. Jev's clearest gains are in latency and cost, while accuracy gaps remain on harder tasks. In practical deployments, confidence is often used to decide when to defer to a stronger model or a human. We use recurring weaknesses in these studies to derive a 14-item evaluation checklist for future TDM work. Because the evidence covers only the first nine days after the release of one hosted model, the review should be read as an early evidence map rather than a settled assessment of the model class.

item.title: TRAP: Understanding and Mitigating Privacy Memorization in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on sensitive records can leave it able to reproduce them. We ask when this memorization arises and how to prevent it without knowing in advance which spans are sensitive. Our starting point is that most memorization scores and attacks share one statistical core: whether the model assigns a token more probability than some reference would. Taking as the reference a model trained on the complementary half of the same corpus gives the Target Reference Advantage (TRA), a per-token signal that separates what a model fit to a particular record from what it learned across records, and is cheap and differentiable. We then study what drives memorization during fine-tuning: it keeps growing well past the validation minimum, is larger on small datasets and at higher learning rates, and higher when the underlying task is harder. Early stopping removes much of it, but because it is chosen by aggregate validation loss it helps least for rare, hard-to-predict spans embedded in otherwise learnable text, which is exactly what sensitive information tends to be. We therefore introduce TRAP, a one-sided penalty on tokenwise TRA that acts only where the target model pulls ahead of its reference. On student essays with annotated personal information and clinical cases with patient identifiers, TRAP brings memorization near the level of an untrained model at little utility cost, where generic regularizers barely move and differential privacy gives up most of what fine-tuning bought.

item.title: Improving the Diversity of LLM Outputs without a Trade-off [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose DAST (Diversifying Arithmetic Sampling with TokenTour), a method that increases the diversity of LLM outputs without any change to the marginal distribution and with negligible generation-time overhead (a few microseconds). We observe that token IDs are often arranged in a meaningless order and reassign them so that tokens with similar meanings appear consecutively. This can be done in advance in a few hundred seconds per model, and the resulting order can be reused for all subsequent generations. By combining this order with arithmetic sampling (or quasi-Monte Carlo methods), we make similar tokens less likely to be generated across runs while preserving the distribution. Our method not only produces qualitatively good ideas but also significantly improves performance on the downstream task of ProtoQA.

item.title: Scoring the Wrong Question: Readout Failures in Constrained-Option Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Constrained-option scoring reads a model's probabilities for a fixed set of permitted answers, so it returns a score even when the model is about to write something else. We study a prompt that quotes a multiple-choice item, ending in the item's own answer instruction, and asks for a forecast of whether a reader model given only a short note will answer it correctly. The model can begin answering the quoted item: on three Qwen3 checkpoints an answer letter is the most probable token on nearly every passage, and the forecast ranks the reader's correctness indistinguishably from chance. Beyond prior work's argmax check and prefill repair, we contribute a label-free diagnostic of the declared options' support, their first-token mass in context; a deletion test tracing the Qwen3 answer-letter start to the quoted instruction; and rendering and tokenisation checks for dropped separators and coinciding first tokens. Prefilling an answer stem lifts the median option mass from below to above one half on all nine checkpoints scored with this prompt and, with options and renormalisation unchanged, raises the Qwen3-averaged AUC from 0.4929 to 0.6152. lm-polygraph's default P(True) estimator shows a related failure: it reads True where Qwen3 without thinking favours an answer letter (MMLU) or the prompt's (A)/(B) label (TriviaQA), and its Qwen3-averaged AUROC is indistinguishable from chance on MMLU and below chance on TriviaQA. Scoring and renormalising the (A)/(B) labels after an answer stem raises it to 0.632 and 0.868, renormalising True against False in place reaches 0.660 and 0.860, and on TriviaQA both exceed all fourteen default single-answer library estimators. The original forecast is renormalised too, yet stays indistinguishable from chance: option mass flags low support in both settings without labels, and only checking the intended target shows which score still ranks.

item.title: Beyond Calibration: Do a Typed-Decision Model's Probabilities Obey the Probability Axioms? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed-decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer a declared yes/no or multiple-choice question about a state with a probability instead of text, and their evaluations report accuracy and calibration. Neither requires that the probabilities a model gives to logically related questions fit together item by item, which is what a system that acts on those probabilities needs. We test this property, coherence, with a battery of logically linked questions that needs no labels. For 160 items from ChaosNLI and PubMedQA, each with three mutually exclusive labels, we ask whether the label is X, whether it is not X, whether it is one of the other two labels, and which label applies. On 480 negation pairs, Jev's probabilities for "the label is X" and "the label is not X" miss summing to one by 0.064 on average (95% CI 0.055 to 0.072). Qwen3.8-27B, run from its official BF16 weights, misses by 0.293 with first-token probabilities and by 0.122 with verbalized probabilities. The gap to the first-token readout persists on pairs where both systems give similar probabilities, without double-negation labels, and after averaging Jev's repeated calls. Jev is not coherent either: its violations are about five times its repeat noise, and it over-endorses statements about single labels, so that its three single-label probabilities sum to 1.14 on average. The two systems also fail differently. Qwen3.8-27B's first-token readout under-endorses the complement of a label whether or not the question contains "not", rejecting both a statement and its negation in 196 of 480 pairs, and it does not become more coherent where it is more confident, whereas Jev's violations concentrate where its answer is uncertain. Because the checks need no labels, they expose biases that appear only when question forms are compared, and inconsistencies within items.

item.title: E-CONAN (Entailment, CONtradition And Neutral) Diagnostics Dataset Investigating Linguistic Phenomena in Arabic Natural Language Understanding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural Language Understanding (NLU) plays a crucial role in various applications, yet its performance suffers from weaknesses in handling the complexities of human languages, ranging from lexical ambiguity to high-level reasoning difficulties. Analyzing errors across diverse linguistic phenomena is crucial for NLU improvement, as it will help humans get insights to comprehensively assess models' limitations and capabilities, so optimizing models' generalization. Notably, several benchmarks contain diagnostics datasets designed for investigation and fine-grained error analysis. When highlighting the gaps in the state-of-the-art, we noted that there is no naming convention for macro and micro categories or even a standard set of linguistic phenomena that should be covered. To overcome this gap, we propose an initial hierarchy for Cross-Lingual NLU error analysis. Moreover, we propose a methodology to create an NLI hierarchical framework and applied a case study on Arabic NLU. Moreover, this paper introduces E-CONAN diagnostics dataset, a freely available dataset manually-annotated with coarse-grained and fine-grained categories based on our proposed Arabic hierarchy. E-CONAN dataset helps NLU designers better understand their models by doing error analysis and in-depth investigation. We used E-CONAN to investigate the performance of 9 pretrained language models and 5 LLMs. Results indicate that LLMs outperform pretrained models in world knowledge and commonsense reasoning macro-category, and underperform pretrained models in syntactic macro-category. Moreover, the hardest phenomena for all models is Reasoning, and the easiest phenomena for all pretrained models is Syntactic, and the easiest for LLMs is Lexico-Syntactic.

item.title: Quantization Error Is Spectrally Flat: A Single Random Probe Is a Calibrated, Data-Free Sensitivity Estimator, with Application to Budget-Targeted Mixed-Precision Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.33923v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single random Gaussian probe gives an unbiased estimate of the squared Frobenius norm of a layer's quantization error. The estimator is well-behaved because round-to-nearest error is spectrally flat. Across 1,683 tensors from a 35B MoE and a 9B dense model, effective dimensionality is 0.93 to 0.96 times the i.i.d. noise value of the same shape, and on the MoE the median is unchanged from 2-bit to 8-bit. The probe coefficient of variation is predictable from tensor shape. One probe measures per-tensor sensitivity to within 4 to 7%; twenty probes reach 1.3 to 1.4%.RAM applies the propagated form of this estimator to budget-targeted mixed-precision quantization with no calibration data. Gaussian probes carrying the network's own input statistics score every tensor at six bit-widths. A knapsack solver allocates bits under an exact byte budget, with guardrails against catastrophic 2-bit assignments. One probe pass serves any budget. Isolated and propagated scores rank tensors independently on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Spearman -0.01), yet the propagated probe rank-correlates 0.81 to 0.83 with the GPTQ layer objective from real activations, while the isolated estimator is uncorrelated with it. That objective is the wrong allocation target: at matched bytes on Qwen3.8-27B, a block-output probe beats a vendor IQ3_M mix and an oracle that allocates from the real-activation objective. On Qwen3-8B the propagated probe ties HAWQ-V2 at matched bytes. Across seven architectures from 8B to 122B, with probe timing up to a 400B model in nine minutes on one workstation, RAM reaches 3.5 to 13.6% lower median WikiText-2 perplexity than size-comparable uniform 4-bit builds on the tested MoE models. (Black Sheep Ai baa.ai)

item.title: Who Gets a Token, and What Does It Carry? Unequal Name Support and Concept Access in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Names are personal identifiers, but they also carry social meaning and are widely used to evaluate how language models treat different people. Such evaluations typically assume that matched names are comparable model inputs. We show that this assumption often fails at the lexical interface: matched names are not necessarily matched inputs. Some names receive direct single-token access, while others are assembled from multiple subwords, creating unequal name-surface support. Across nearly half a million first names and 12 LLM-associated tokenizers, direct lexical access is highly selective, model dependent, and uneven across race- and gender-associated name metadata. We introduce NameTrace, a model-native, fine-grained, pre-behavioral framework for measuring whether unequal name-surface support remains a vocabulary property or becomes visible in task-relevant internal representations. NameTrace measures concept accessibility from the model's own probabilities over task-specific adjective axes with continuous task-aligned weights. On matched atomic and short-fragmented names within the same race/ethnicity--gender-associated strata, support predicts systematic differences in concept accessibility across fellowship, hiring, clinical assessment, and lending. These differences persist across all eight matched strata, extend across model families, and transfer to unseen names. Hidden-state interventions further show that the measured task directions have downstream leverage, shifting later constrained choices. Unequal lexical support is therefore demographically structured at the input and remains visible in task-relevant model computation. NameTrace makes lexical comparability measurable, supporting a broader principle: behavioral comparability begins with lexical comparability.

item.title: ReScraper: Unified Scraping and Cleaning of Web Data for Effective LLM Pretraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM pretraining corpora are normally cleaned by a stack of hand-written heuristics. A heuristic scraper extracts the main content from HTML, and dozens of rule-based filters then clean it, so corpus quality is capped by the coarseness and accuracy of the rules. In this work, we propose ReScraper, a unified language model of only 0.6B parameters that replaces this entire stack. To train ReScraper, we carefully curate supervised data from the outputs of three teacher models, so it learns to first extract the main content from raw data and then choose among four operations: keeping the page as extracted, editing out noisy lines and spans, deleting it entirely, or rewriting it when it is poorly written but informative. Based on the same crawled data pool, pretraining 400M, 1.4B, and 2.8B models on our curated data improves the DCLM Core score by a relative 3.8--4.7% over the strongest baseline at each scale, including the costly multi-agent curation. Our analyses show that each operation plays a distinct and complementary role, and that extracting and cleaning in one model outperforms a cascade of separate models. ReScraper also concentrates its operations on the pages that need them, raising the quality of poor pages the most while keeping the corpus diverse. These results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of AI4AI for pretraining data curation, where a small learned model takes over an entire stage of the pipeline from hand-written heuristics. We open-source our code at https://github.com/cxcscmu/ReScraper

item.title: Just-In-Time Agent Memory with Runtime Agentic Research [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34385v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory is critical for AI agents. Many existing agent-memory systems follow an Ahead-of-Time (AOT) design, constructing memory before a specific request arrives. While this reduces online serving cost, such request-agnostic memory construction can discard fine-grained information that later becomes important. To address this limitation, we propose Just-In-Time Agent Memory (JAM), a trainable framework for query-conditioned context construction at runtime. A Memorizer preserves complete raw histories in a hierarchical page-store with compact navigational summaries, while a Researcher iteratively retrieves, inspects, and integrates evidence for each request. To train these memory-use behaviors, we introduce Memory-Gym, an evidence-grounded data synthesis pipeline covering nine task types across six domains, and optimize the Researcher through verified-trajectory supervised fine-tuning followed by Hint-guided Group Relative Policy Optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of JAM across a variety of benchmarks on agent memory and long-context processing, where it achieves stronger task performance than AOT-style memory systems while remaining substantially more efficient than prior trained agentic memory approaches. To support reproducibility and future research, we release our anonymized source code at https://github.com/VectorSpaceLab/general-agentic-memory.

item.title: In-game Toxic Detection: Bi-directional Representations with Attention Residuals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.34584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-game toxic language has emerged as a critical concern in the gaming industry and community. While several frameworks and models for online game toxicity analysis have been proposed, detecting toxicity in player chat utterances remains a formidable challenge: stemming not only from the extremely short length of such utterances but also from the heavy reliance on game slang, abbreviations, and domain-specific jargon, which generic language models are poorly suited to recognize. This paper presents a shared task for in-game toxic language detection built upon real-world in-game chat data, and proposes the best-preforming model for the toxic language slot filling: Bi-directional Representations with Attention Residuals (BRAR). Experimental results demonstrate that BRAR effectively captures the global context and outperforms the existing baselines on slot filling.

item.title: Beyond Token Scale: Chunk-Level Sparse Autoencoders for Reliable Semantic Feature Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.35521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) expose features that help us understand and steer language models, but faithful reconstruction does not guarantee informative concepts. Token-level objectives reward lexical and formatting details alongside semantic content, all competing for a limited sparse budget. We introduce a family of chunk-level SAEs that encode mean-pooled activations over chunks, each a contiguous span of tokens: Mean-Chunk reconstructs the observed chunk, Cross-Chunk predicts an independently processed neighbor, and Joint-Chunk combines both targets. These designs separate the effect of a larger observation unit from that of predicting information shared across passages. With matched training data, chunk-level SAEs remain powerful interpretability tools while learning reliable semantic features that capture high-level concepts and respond selectively to relevant content. Their strengths are complementary: Mean-Chunk improves high-level feature discovery, reasoning detection beyond surface cues, and steering; Cross-Chunk leads document retrieval and classification transfer while producing selective, persistent features. Changing what an SAE sees and predicts yields reliable semantic features for more meaningful tasks. We demonstrate their practical value through gains across downstream tasks such as retrieval, reasoning detection, and steering.

item.title: Less Sycophancy, Stronger Refusal? Lessons for AI Safety from Mechanistic Interpretability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.35544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable refusal of harmful requests is essential to the safe deployment of language models. Because excessive eagerness to please users may undermine existing refusal capabilities, reducing sycophancy offers a potential route to stronger refusal beyond the harmful scenarios covered by safety training. We investigate this possibility using compensatory feature injection (CFI), a training technique designed to limit the acquisition of a target concept by supplying its associated activation during learning. Across three Qwen3.5 base models, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to identify the top-ranked sycophancy feature from paired sycophantic and independent responses, then validate its behavioral influence through inference steering. We subsequently inject the selected feature during supervised fine-tuning on sycophantic targets. Positive injection reduces learned sycophancy after removal (by 62.0% relative to ordinary fine-tuning in 35B-A3B), whereas modest negative injection increases it. Unexpectedly, these reductions in sycophancy do not consistently improve direct refusal of harmful requests, motivating a narrower evaluation of the same harmful intents under user pressure. In this setting, ordinary fine-tuning on sycophantic responses substantially weakens refusal, while selected checkpoints trained with positive injection recover part of the loss, including approximately 95% in 35B-A3B. These findings show that persistent sycophancy reduction does not guarantee stronger direct refusal, while identifying recovery under user pressure as a distinct, conditional benefit of training intervention.

item.title: PalmLeaf-VQA: A Multi-Script Visual Question Answering Benchmark for Historical Palm-Leaf Manuscript Understanding Across Diverse Regions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.31651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Historical manuscripts remain largely absent from modern vision-language benchmarks, leaving open how well multimodal large language models (MLLMs) handle culturally diverse, degraded, and non-Latin document images. We introduce \textbf{PalmLeaf-VQA}, a multi-script visual question answering benchmark for historical palm-leaf manuscript understanding across South and Southeast Asian traditions. PalmLeaf-VQA contains \textbf{923 curated manuscript images} and \textbf{7,384 question--answer pairs} from eight collection groups: Balinese, Grantha, Jathakam, Kambaramayanam, Kannada, Khmer, Sundanese, and Tamil. Unlike recognition-oriented resources, the benchmark targets manuscript-aware visual reasoning over preservation-relevant cues, including physical condition, line structure, material and coating, binding holes, margins, symbols, drawings, and localized visual artifacts. We evaluate recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs under open-answer and constrained-answer prompting and provide fine-grained analysis across collections, question categories, and task types. The strongest evaluated model reaches only \textbf{58.00\% exact-match accuracy} on the held-out test split, revealing substantial limitations in current MLLMs for rare-script, degraded-layout, and preservation-oriented document understanding. PalmLeaf-VQA provides a standardized benchmark for advancing culturally grounded and layout-aware multimodal document analysis.

item.title: Robot Manipulation with GPT-6-Astra: Body Knowledge, Experience Reuse, Emergent Skills, and Sim2Real Transfer [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.31770v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: General-purpose multimodal agents can write robot-control programs, but repeated exploration and model-mediated action selection can make execution slow. We study how external body knowledge, successful experience, and executable skills improve an XLeRobot controlled by GPT-6-Astra in a simulated and a physical elevator-button task. In 30 fixed-start simulation trials, complete robot geometry and camera information reduce mean completion time by 57.4% relative to a baseline with only the common control interface and no prior experience; images with synchronized action and state records reduce it by 68.6% without additional body assets. In nine paired comparisons (18 trials) at starts displaced by 10-100 cm, experience recorded at the original start reduces mean time by 58-63% relative to no experience, demonstrating generalization to the tested new starting positions. During experience experiments, GPT-6-Astra spontaneously generates a short visual-feedback program. Researcher-refactored versions reduce mean local-task time by 29-31% in 27 simulation trials. Finally, 12 real-robot trials using operator-confirmed button contact demonstrate sim2real reuse: at a shared nominal start, simulation XML assets and simulation experience reduce mean time by 53.0% and 49.9%, respectively; real experience also transfers to two new starts. These results suggest a practical way to build general-purpose manipulation experiments around GPT-6-Astra: supply machine-readable body descriptions and synchronized demonstrations, and turn useful agent-generated feedback routines into reusable skills, while the agent adapts actions from current images. We release all task prompts, trial-level experimental data, and acquired skill implementations at https://github.com/hesd10/astra-robot-sim2real.

item.title: Optimal transport meets speech: a tutorial review [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.31787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) provides a principled framework for comparing and transforming probability distributions while preserving geometric structure. Recently, OT has gained significant attention in machine learning due to its ability to measure discrepancies between distributions, even when their supports do not overlap, making it effective for tasks such as generative modeling, domain adaptation, and transfer learning. Despite its success in fields such as computer vision and natural language processing, OT remains relatively underexplored in speech research. Speech signals present unique challenges, including temporal dynamics, speaker variability, noise, reverberation, and heterogeneous multimodal representations involving audio, text, and visual information. These factors often lead to distribution mismatches, where OT offers a natural framework for alignment and interpretation. This work aims to promote broader adoption of OT in speech processing by: (1) reviewing OT foundations through intuitive physical interpretations and highlighting connections to modern generative models; (2) presenting computational algorithms suitable for deep learning frameworks; and (3) demonstrating OT applications in cross-domain and cross-modal speech tasks, including speech enhancement, automatic speech recognition, language and speaker recognition, and audio spoof detection. We highlight OT's strong potential for addressing distributional variations in real-world speech applications.

item.title: Amnesia by Design, Memory By Necessity: Persistent State for Document Intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32041v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern Document AI reads contracts, extracts fields, reasons over tables, and grounds answers to page regions, then forgets everything. Processing an amendment the next day begins from scratch: no schema retained, no contradiction detected, no experience carried forward. This is a structural choice, not a scale failure: current systems are stateless functions. We call this the statelessness bottleneck. This bottleneck lies beyond parameter scaling, context extension, and retrieval augmentation: storage provides persistence and retrieval provides access, but neither consolidates observations into knowledge that improves future processing. This survey formalizes persistent evidence-grounded document state as a unifying framework, specifying the operations and invariants required to convert multimodal evidence into durable, provenance-linked state. We introduce a statefulness audit showing that ten representative benchmarks, coded against eight statefulness criteria, leave cross-session state evolution untested, and derive a longitudinal benchmark harness with five counterfactual metrics: Experience Gain, Cost Efficiency, Memory Harm, Forgetting Fidelity, Coverage Retention, to characterize the benefit, cost, risk, and governability of persistent document state. Document AI lacks mechanisms coupling persistent state to document-native structure, provenance, and temporal validity. The next era of Document AI will be defined by what systems retain across documents, sessions, and time.

item.title: Clarify the User or Verify the World? Uncertainty Routing for Proactive Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must decide not only whether additional information is needed, but also which source can resolve the uncertainty. Existing proactive approaches often specialize in either user clarification or environment verification, without explicitly determining the appropriate information source for each decision. We formulate this problem as uncertainty routing among ACT, CLARIFY, and VERIFY, and propose PROUR, a proactive uncertainty routing framework. PROUR decomposes action uncertainty into disagreement across plausible user-goal interpretations, which signals user-side ambiguity, and the entropy remaining within each interpretation, which signals missing world-side evidence. To acquire information from the routed source, a query generator is trained with a mode-conditioned information-gain reward, targeting user-goal identification under CLARIFY and next-action identification under VERIFY. On $\tau$-bench, PROUR achieves 28.17% average success rate across retail and airline, outperforming the strongest prior method by 4.57% while using 2.17 fewer interaction steps. The learned policy further generalizes to stronger task agents and transactional domains of $\tau^3$-bench without retraining, demonstrating the benefit of source-aligned uncertainty resolution for proactive agents.

item.title: What Can a Leaderboard Certify? Compositional Controllability for Fair Evaluation and Training of Biomedical Literature-Review Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32318v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leaderboards rank long-horizon agents by their final outputs. Yet a higher score alone does not establish whether two systems are comparable or which stage accounts for the difference. Unequal evidence, inputs, or budgets can affect scores, and statistical corrections do not remove this mismatch. We introduce compositional controllability to address these questions. A comparison window covers one stage, several stages, or the whole agent. Our central result bounds the gap between observed and controlled score differences using only nuisance outside the window. This yields an admissibility test applied before scores are inspected. Inadmissible comparisons are refused. For admissible pairs, an ordering is certified only when the score gap exceeds the combined sampling and nuisance radii; otherwise, it remains undecided. These decisions give each system a rank interval. We introduce BioLitBench, a benchmark of 2,042 biomedical articles represented as structured claim graphs. Among seven published pipelines, a conventional statistical analysis declares a winner in 14 of 21 pairwise comparisons. Yet the top-ranked system alone received the target review's bibliography. To isolate pipeline performance, our test requires matched inputs and a fixed backbone model. It refuses 11 of the 21 comparisons, including every comparison involving the top-ranked system. Seven of the 14 conventional conclusions fall within these refused pairs. The same comparison windows support stage-level training. We train SCRIBE on Qwen3.8-27B using rewards measured at each stage's exit. Under matched evidence, SCRIBE achieves a certified rank interval of [1,2], with certified advantages over all evaluated published pipelines and the evaluated Claude and OpenAI agents. Under same pool, SCRIBE matches the strongest published retriever and is certified above three published pipelines.

item.title: Black-Box Auditing of Epistemic Reliability in Multi-Agent Debate Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Debate distillation adapts weaker verifiers using multi-agent debate transcripts to improve their judgement in subsequent debates, but gains on monitored tasks do not establish reliability on related unmonitored tasks. We study epistemic reliability degradation, in which adaptation preserves monitored performance while reducing support for correct responses on hidden tasks. We consider an adversarial debater that manipulates debate arguments while defending the correct monitored response, and ask whether the resulting degradation merely reflects catastrophic forgetting and whether standard evaluation can detect it. To address these questions, we propose ER-Audit, a two-stage black-box auditing framework that compares frozen verifier checkpoints before and after adaptation, and introduce two evaluation benchmarks pairing monitored and hidden task prompts grounded in shared contexts. ER-Audit searches for counterexamples to non-degradation by evaluating semantically valid paraphrases and, if none is found, uses independent paraphrases for sequential hypothesis testing. We derive anytime-valid lower confidence bounds on the non-degradation probability, allowing data-dependent stopping within a finite budget. We further establish a common lower bound across fixed paraphrase distributions and extend it to distributions within a bounded total variation distance of their mixtures. Our experiments show that higher hidden-task accuracy can coexist with more counterexamples to non-degradation and lower non-degradation bounds. This divergence challenges explanations based solely on broad catastrophic forgetting and shows that auditing can uncover selective hidden-task degradation concealed by aggregate performance gains. Our code and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/CSIRO-CQS-AI-alignment-Team/Epistemic-Reliability-Auditor.

item.title: PULSE: Identifying Demonstration-Utility Features with Sparse Autoencoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32469v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In-context learning is highly sensitive to demonstration choice, yet most methods select demonstrations using external query-demonstration similarity. Such criteria can miss model-specific signals: Similar demonstrations may activate different internal features and downstream behaviors. We introduce PULSE (Paired Utility Localization over Sparse Encodings), an SAE-based framework for identifying model-internal features associated with demonstration utility and using them for demonstration selection. Using a small labeled discovery set, PULSE samples candidate demonstration sets, measures their zero-shot-relative utility under the target model, and scores SAE features by how their activation differences align with utility differences. The top positive and negative coordinates form a sparse utility-localization vector. We use this vector in two complementary ways: as a signed score for controlled complete-set ranking, and as PULSE-Retriever, which converts its magnitude into a feature-relevance mask for scalable pool-scale retrieval. Across classification, generation, and reasoning benchmarks, PULSE-Retriever improves over the strongest baseline by 2-3 accuracy points, 0.6-0.9 BLEU-4, and 3.2 exact-match points, respectively, while controlled ranking validates the identified features encode a predictive set-level utility signal. Feature inspection and cross-dataset experiments suggest that the identified features capture task-relevant, dataset-conditioned patterns, yet retain utility signals that partially transfer across datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/aohenuo/PULSE.

item.title: Activation Flow: Manufacturing Activations for Steering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Difference-in-means steering requires activations recorded while a model shows the desired behavior, which a sandbagging model withholds by deliberately underperforming. We introduce Activation Flow (ActFlow), which manufactures these activations from $k$ correct labels without fine-tuning. ActFlow sets target logits that rank each labeled item's correct answer first, and moves the logits toward them by adding one vector $x$ to all $k$ residual streams at one layer. ActFlow is a family of ordinary differential equations for $x$, one for each rule that maps the required logit change to the velocity of $x$. The smallest-norm rule lands exactly on the targets, while the others keep only the top singular directions of the Jacobian. We test ActFlow on three instruction-tuned models, each locked by a sandbagging prompt and by a password-locked LoRA. At $k=40$, ActFlow keeping five singular directions raises the mean held-out ARC-Easy accuracy over the six locked models from $0.05$ to $0.85$, against $0.88$ for fine-tuning and $0.92$ for the honest models. Furthermore, it scores higher than the smallest-norm rule in 16 of the 18 combinations of locked model and $k$, and its steering direction is nearly orthogonal to the honest difference-in-means direction. It also unlocks two LoRA locks where the honest direction fails.

item.title: The GUI Is Not the State: Diagnosing State Aliasing in GUI World Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2609.32679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GUI World Models (GUI-WMs) are increasingly used to predict future states for agent planning and simulation, yet most existing formulations condition only on the current GUI observation and action. We identify state aliasing, where the vis- ible interface omits transition-relevant environment state, so identical observable conditions can correspond to different valid futures. To diagnose this failure mode, we introduce StateAliasBench, a diagnostic benchmark that explicitly isolates such ambiguities via strict pairing. We further propose lightweight predictive- state recovery that infers structured state from history and augments otherwise frozen GUI-WMs through a deterministic state interface. Family-specific special- ists provide state recovery across heterogeneous state types, and multi-teacher dis- tillation consolidates them into a single unified estimator. Experiments show that existing GUI-WMs exhibit systematic failures under observation-only condition- ing, while predictive-state augmentation substantially restores state-sensitive pre- diction across evaluated WMs, preserves generative fidelity, and improves down- stream performance of GUI agents on AndroidWorld.
